newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Heavy fighting erupts as Zaire rebels turn up heat.
newsitem.headline: Heavy fighting erupts as Zaire rebels turn up heat.

text.p: Heavy fighting flared around the eastern Zaire town of Goma on Thursday as Tutsi rebels sought to consolidate gains over their Hutu foes ahead of the arrival of a multinational peace force.

Underlining the hazards awaiting a U.N. intervention force, firing from mortar, anti-aircraft and machineguns boomed around the teeming Mugunga camp about 10 km (six miles) west of the rebel-held town on Rwanda's border.
Goma residents said they believed the rebels were trying to take on the Hutu fighters before the arrival of the Canadian-led force, with a powerful U.S. military contingent, in a few days.
Some estimates say Mugunga is now home to 400,000 Hutu refugees, or one-third of the Rwandan and Burundian Hutus scattered in eastern Zaire by a month-long rebellion.

After four weeks of mounting crisis, the Western powers have agreed to take action in Central Africa, but have stressed it would be a strictly humanitarian mission to help more than one million refugees and displaced Zaireans.

But even before setting foot in the Great Lakes region, home to an explosive cocktail of mixed ethnic and political conflicts, differences emerged over whether the mission could succeed with such limited aims.
The head of the U.N.'s food aid arm said on Thursday that force must separate "the bad guys with the guns" from starving refugees or its mission would have to be repeated.

Catherine Bertini, executive director of the World Food Programme (WFP), also said that while the first step would be seeing that no weapons interfered with humanitarian work, ultimately fighters would have to be disarmed.

"The step necessary for peace in the long term is disarmament but if we're talking about keeping people alive and feeding people today we would want to separate the bad guys with the guns from the people who need to live today," she said.
White House press secretary Mike McCurry said Washington believed the mission would have to be clearly defined and not try to disarm militants or conduct any kind of forced entry.
But regional experts say that without taking on board Hutu thugs, blamed for the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, the humanitarian side of the mission will fail.

Former members of the Rwandan government army and dreaded Interahamwe militia massacred an estimated 800,000 people, mostly minority Tutsis, before taking sanctuary with thousands of other Hutus after Rwanda's Tutsis won power and stopped the killing.

"This is a false start. As long as the international force is not prepared to disarm the ex-FAR (army troops) and the Interahamwe its objectives will not be achieved," Seth Kamanzi, an adviser to the Rwandan president, said.

McCurry said the U.S. commitment, expected to last about four months, involved sending 1,000 ground troops to Zaire. An additional 2,000 to 3,000 American troops would go to nearby countries to help with support activities, the Pentagon said.
The world community is eager to avoid a re-run of 1994 when it ended up feeding many of those responsible for the slaughter in Rwanda.

They then intimidated their kinsmen against returning and turned the camps into military bases for a possible comeback, infuriating the Tutsi-led governments of Rwanda and Burundi and sowing the seeds of the present crisis.
Equally, the major powers do not want a repeat of the disastrous Somalia experience in 1993 where the U.S. suffered high casualties in a futile attempt to apprehend one warlord.
"It is an impossible circle to square," said one regional expert, warning of the dangers of "action in a political vacuum".
France, Spain and several African countries, including South Africa, have all said they will also send troops.

The French, deeply distrusted by Tutsis in the region for their financial and military support to Rwanda's now-discredited former Hutu government, said on Thursday they hoped the first troops would be in Zaire by the weekend.
A U.S. assessment team of more than 40 arrived in the Rwandan capital Kigali from Uganda on Thursday to check out conditions on the ground for logistical support.
